title: Loot
synopsis: Your husband cheated. The divorce settlement gave you eighty-seven billion dollars. Your foundation has a staff of six and a board of one — you — and you don't know what an audit is. Start there.

nodes.text: Noon, and you arrive at the Wells Foundation still in the yacht clothes from Wednesday. Sofia hands you a coffee in a paper cup, which you accept the way a person accepts a live animal. There is a whiteboard. The whiteboard has goals on it, in bullet points, and one of the bullet points is about you.

choices.text: Pretend you already know everything
choices.consequence: You nod through forty minutes of acronyms and write the word metrics on a legal pad in your own handwriting, which does not clarify anything.

choices.text: Ask Sofia to walk you through everything
choices.consequence: You admit you do not know what a program officer is. Sofia's face does something complicated and settles, eventually, on relieved.

nodes.text: Three morning shows in one day. Somewhere on the parkway it occurs to you that a person is going to ask, on camera, how it feels to give away a fortune, and that your entire answer at present is the word great with a question mark after it. Sofia reads the briefing packet aloud. You look at a bridge.

choices.text: Wing it and hope you sound human
choices.consequence: You get through two shows on charm and lose the third by describing eighty-seven billion dollars as, honestly, a lot of money. It trends.

choices.text: Pre-write three honest sentences
choices.consequence: You draft three sentences in the car and deliver them slightly wrong on air, which makes them sound true. Sofia texts one word: better.

nodes.text: Howard the accountant will not make eye contact for ten minutes, then discovers you have no idea what any of this means, and relaxes completely. He walks you down the line items with the cap of a pen. You ask what overhead is. He tells you. You ask why everybody in the building says it like a slur.

choices.text: Make Howard your real guide
choices.consequence: You start bringing your questions to Howard instead of to the room, which quietly reorganizes the whole power structure of the third floor.

choices.text: Buy Howard a better office chair first
choices.consequence: A twelve-hundred-dollar chair arrives Thursday. Howard sits in it for a year and mentions it to every single person who walks past his desk.

nodes.text: The director gives you the tour she gives every donor. Intake, kitchen, bed count, the wall of thank-you drawings taped at child height. She names the foundation twice and does not recognize your face once. You built this with a divorce settlement and you are being walked past a mop closet like a stranger.

choices.text: Tell her who you are
choices.consequence: You give her your name and watch the tour change temperature. The rest of it is warmer, smoother, and considerably less useful to you.

choices.text: Stay anonymous, observe
choices.consequence: You keep your mouth shut for ninety minutes and learn what the intake line actually sounds like at four in the afternoon on a Thursday.

nodes.text: A photograph of you on a deck in Sardinia holding a coupe of champagne, captioned rough day, resurfaces the morning after a flood takes half a county in Mississippi. The photo is four years old. Nobody cares that the photo is four years old. Sofia's phone begins making a sound you have never heard a phone make.

choices.text: Apologize in your own words on camera
choices.consequence: You record it on a phone in a stairwell with no styling and no lighting, say the wrong thing twice and the right thing once, and it holds.

choices.text: Donate aggressively to the flood relief
choices.consequence: You wire forty million before lunch and the story becomes billionaire buys forgiveness, which is not inaccurate, and stings for exactly that reason.

nodes.text: Nicholas has driven you three hundred times and you know two facts about him. He acts. He has a callback Thursday that he is not going to bring up, because he assumes you would rather not hear about it. He is also the only person this month who has told you something you did not want to hear.

choices.text: Promote Nicholas to assistant
choices.consequence: You give him a desk and a title. He is bad at the job for six weeks and then, without announcement, stops being bad at it.

choices.text: Pay for his class and keep him driving
choices.consequence: You cover the conservatory tuition and he keeps the car, and he cries about it in a parking garage where he believes you cannot see him.

nodes.text: Arthur runs operations, is fifty, is divorced, and carries the specific patience of a man who has watched several very rich people walk into this building and discover they were the point of their own charity. He does not flatter you. He explains things twice without making it a favor. You find him mildly terrifying.

choices.text: Ask Arthur to be your sponsor at the foundation
choices.consequence: You ask him to tell you when you are being an idiot. He agrees instantly and without negotiation, which should probably have alarmed you.

choices.text: Date Arthur for one bad month
choices.consequence: Four weeks of dinners where he is careful and you are performing. You end it in a parking lot and both of you are audibly relieved.

nodes.text: John calls. He has been in therapy a year and has been given, you can hear it, a script. He apologizes for the assistant, for the lying, for the twenty years. Then comes a pause with a shape to it, and inside that pause is a question about what you are doing with his, with the, with the money.

choices.text: Take the apology, refuse the conversation
choices.consequence: You accept the apology and hang up before the second half arrives. Your hands shake for a while afterward, which irritates you enormously.

choices.text: Hear him out — over the phone, not in person
choices.consequence: You let him talk for thirty-five minutes and decline to see him. He is still charming. That is the part you had genuinely forgotten.

nodes.text: You and Rhonda take a jet to Vegas and lose ninety thousand dollars to a slot machine that plays a small fanfare every time, plus one hat. Sofia calls at two in the morning. You take it in a bathroom stall, dead sober, listening to your own voice explain, and you hear precisely what you sound like.

choices.text: Call your therapist on the way home
choices.consequence: You book an emergency session from thirty thousand feet and say the word sabotage out loud about yourself for the first time ever.

choices.text: Donate ten million the next morning to compensate
choices.consequence: You wire ten million before breakfast and feel clean for roughly four hours, which appears to be the going rate on that particular purchase.

nodes.text: You ask to be put on the board. Your own board. Sofia has to check her notes to determine whether that is even permitted. It is. Nobody thought you would want it. The first vote you sit through concerns a hundred-million-dollar housing initiative, and you follow eighty percent of it, and eighty percent is new.

choices.text: Vote yes and learn from the consequences
choices.consequence: You vote yes, and fourteen months later two of the four sites are behind schedule, and you make yourself read every quarterly report on both.

choices.text: Vote present and ask better questions
choices.consequence: You abstain and ask four questions instead. Two are stupid. The third one stops the entire room for a full minute.

nodes.text: Sofia is, it turns out, your closest friend, and you know her sister's name from a calendar entry rather than from having asked. You have never been to her apartment. You invite her to a dinner with no agenda attached, and she checks twice whether it is a work dinner, and there is the entire diagnosis.

choices.text: Show up at Sofia's family event this weekend
choices.consequence: You go to a christening in Bay Ridge, drink one beer, hold a baby incorrectly, and are the last guest to leave the building.

choices.text: Send a thoughtful thing instead
choices.consequence: You have something perfect and expensive delivered to her. It is perfect. It is also a very elegant method of not going.

nodes.text: Six months in, you read the mission statement aloud in a meeting and discover it means nothing whatsoever. So you say a different one out loud: end family homelessness in two states inside ten years. The room goes quiet in a new way. Sofia stares. Arthur, at the far end of the table, does not stop smiling.

choices.text: Push the new mission to the board
choices.consequence: You take it to the board whole and it passes with one dissent, and the dissent turns out to be the most useful person in the room.

choices.text: Pilot it in one city first
choices.consequence: You start in one city, which is slower and correct, and which means any visible win is now four years further away than you wanted.

nodes.text: You move Howard out of accounting and into program strategy. He asks whether he is in trouble. Monday he is outside your office at seven with a binder of twenty-eight slides he built over the weekend, and slide one is titled Where The Money Could Actually Go, and slide nine is genuinely upsetting.

choices.text: Adopt half his slides immediately
choices.consequence: You green-light fourteen of them where you stand. Howard goes back to his desk and sits down very carefully, like the chair might not hold him.

choices.text: Make him present to the board next Tuesday
choices.consequence: He presents in a suit newer than the binder, sweats through the whole thing, and fields a question from the board's hardest member perfectly.

nodes.text: Midnight, and John is on the intercom at the gate, drunk, wanting to talk. On the monitor he looks like the man you married rather than the man you spent twenty years becoming smaller alongside. There is a real difference between those two people, and tonight, in grainy black and white, you can see it.

choices.text: Send him home in his own car
choices.consequence: You put him in the back of his own car, go inside, and do not look at the monitor again. You sleep fine, which surprises you.

choices.text: Talk to him for one hour, then send him home
choices.consequence: You give him one hour at the kitchen island. He is funny for forty minutes and sad for twenty and gone by two in the morning.

nodes.text: First gala under the new mission. Four hundred guests, a seating chart with a small war behind it, and a speech you have written and thrown out nine separate times. Arthur sits in the second row attempting to look like a man attending a work function. The teleprompter is loaded. Your hands are cold.

choices.text: Throw out the speech and speak honestly
choices.consequence: You set the cards down and talk for six minutes about a shelter tour where nobody knew your name. Nobody in the room moves.

choices.text: Stick to the script and let the room cry
choices.consequence: You deliver it flawlessly, exactly as drafted, and it lands, and you feel like a very good instrument being played by somebody else.

nodes.text: Two cities in, the thing is working. Unevenly, slower than the press release claims, more than anybody honestly believed. You have hired people smarter than you and stopped pretending otherwise. You can read a 10-K now. You do it on a Sunday, in reading glasses, with a highlighter, and you do not entirely hate it.

choices.text: Stay engaged for another decade
choices.consequence: You tell Sofia you are not going anywhere and watch her decide whether that is good news. It takes her a full second.

choices.text: Bring on a President so you can step back
choices.consequence: You open the search, and the first candidate asks what you plan to do with your time, and you have nothing ready to say.

nodes.text: Pizza on a marble island in a kitchen designed for a staff of six. Arthur says he likes you. Then he says he does not want to date you, and explains why, and the reasons are not flattering and are all correct. What he wants instead is to be an actual friend for about thirty years.

choices.text: Accept it as the gift it is
choices.consequence: You say yes and mean it, and he takes the last slice, and something in your chest unclenches that you did not know was clenched.

choices.text: Hold out for romance and lose the friendship
choices.consequence: You push for more and get a polite version of the same man for two years, which is a bad trade and one you made yourself.

nodes.text: You write John a letter you never send. It thanks him, genuinely, which is the horrifying part, for leaving, because the settlement paid for a life you had been postponing since you were thirty-one. Four pages. You read it through twice. Forgiveness turns out to be the strangest dividend that money ever produced.

choices.text: Burn the letter; keep the lesson
choices.consequence: You burn it in the sink like a lunatic, set off the smoke alarm, and stand there in all that noise feeling absolutely fine.

choices.text: Donate ten million in his name to spite him
choices.consequence: You put ten million into a housing fund under his full legal name, numeral included. Your lawyer asks whether you are sure. You are.

nodes.text: Sunday. Sofia arrives with two coffees and an actual newspaper, and neither of you mentions work for a full hour. You are sitting on a porch paid for by a man who assumed you would spend the settlement on shoes. Inward or outward. Both are real options now, which they were not four years ago.

choices.text: Keep the next chapter inward
choices.consequence: You decide the next stretch goes to a person nobody is funding, which is you, and it takes a considerable amount of getting used to.

choices.text: Channel the energy outward, even pettily
choices.consequence: You decide the next chapter points outward, and admit to Sofia that roughly fifteen percent of the motivation is straightforward spite.

nodes.text: Family homelessness is down thirty-eight percent across both pilot states, and the number survives three separate audits conducted by people who wanted it not to. Sofia is on the cover of a magazine you have never read. Howard has gone back to accounting because he missed it. You are proud of something that is not your hair.

choices.text: Take the second decade — scale the mission
choices.consequence: You sign for another decade in a conference room with bad overhead lighting, and Arthur brings a cake with the wrong number iced on it.

choices.text: Hand off and become a private donor with opinions
choices.consequence: You name Sofia President, clear your office in ninety minutes, and take exactly one framed thing with you: a photo of a whiteboard.

nodes.text: Somewhere in your fifties you locate the woman John never got around to ruining. She likes early mornings, which is new, and good wine, which is not. She funds a scholarship called For The Late Bloomers, quietly, with no plaque and no gala and no press release, and she signs the check by hand four times a year. She laughs every single time she does it. Nobody has ever asked her why.

The ten million in John's name funds a housing pilot that outperforms his entire foundation on every metric anybody bothers to measure. He calls to congratulate you, warmly and at length, on voicemail. You listen to all of it standing at a window with a coffee going cold in your hand. Then you save the message, which is worse than deleting it, and you know that, and you save it anyway.

You sign on for a second decade. Nine states. Sofia opens London and hires forty people inside a year. Arthur gets a chair that costs more than his first car did. Howard returns to overhead accounting, cheerfully, because overhead accounting is the thing he actually loves. Everyone in this building is now doing the exact job they once fled, came back to, and turned out to be unreasonably good at.

You step back and Sofia takes President and does it better than you managed on your best available day. You become the eccentric in the hat at the back of the gala who writes one careful op-ed a year and accepts no meetings whatsoever. Within four years the foundation has stopped needing you at all. That took some getting used to. It is also, you understand eventually, the entire point.
